corpus_definition: A list of things you can buy.

forms.definition: a book or website that lists goods for sale with pictures and prices
forms.example: My mother ordered a new kettle from the online catalogue.
forms.note: American spelling: catalog.

syn.note: Easy, general word; a catalogue is a list of goods with pictures and prices.
A brochure is a short, thin magazine about a product or a place; a catalogue lists many goods.
A directory lists names, addresses or phone numbers, not goods to buy.

forms.definition: to make a careful list of things, for example in a library or museum
forms.example: The museum staff catalogued every old coin in the collection.
forms.note: Belongs to catalogue = a careful record of items, not a shopping list. American spelling: catalog.
There is no adjective in this family.
There is no adverb in this family.

context.text: My grandmother still likes paper shopping lists, but now she looks at the catalogue on her phone. She found a warm coat in the new winter catalogue and ordered it at once.

reviewer_note: Only one form exists in the shopping meaning; the verb (to record items in a list) is other_meaning.

corpus_definition: to reach someone who is in front of you by moving faster
particle_note: Not separable: 'catch up with someone' (never 'catch someone up with'). Without an object: 'Go on, I'll catch up.' British English also says 'catch someone up'.

relations.note: Reach is general: to get to a person or place; catch up with means you were behind them first.
To overtake is to go past someone; you catch up with them first and then you can overtake them.
More formal; used in sport and racing.
To move more slowly than others so that they get further ahead.

context.text: Aziz stopped to tie his shoe, and the other runners went ahead. He ran very fast and caught up with them near the park. Now he always tells his friends, 'Wait for me, or I will catch up with you!'

reviewer_note: Movement meaning only; 'catch up with' = learn news from a friend or do missed work is a different meaning and is not used here.

corpus_definition: cows and bulls kept on a farm for meat or milk

forms.definition: cows and bulls that farmers keep for meat or milk
forms.example: The farmer moved his cattle to a new field near the river.
forms.note: Cattle is a plural noun with no singular: 'The cattle are hungry.' For one animal, say 'a cow'.

syn.note: Easy, everyday word; cattle also includes bulls.
Livestock means all farm animals: cattle, sheep, goats and horses.
A herd is a group of animals that live together, for example a herd of cattle.

forms.note: There is no verb in this family.
There is no adjective in this family.
There is no adverb in this family.

context.text: My uncle has a small farm near Jizzakh. Every morning he takes his cattle to the hills, and in the evening he brings the cattle home for milking.

reviewer_note: Plural-only noun; no family forms. Compounds (cattleman, cattle market) left out by rule 7.

corpus_definition: To make something happen, usually a bad event.

forms.definition: the person or thing that makes something happen
forms.example: The police are trying to find the cause of the fire.
forms.note: Another meaning, 'an idea people support' (a good cause, give money to a cause), is not this map.

syn.note: Easy word; reason often explains why someone did something, cause is what made it happen.
The place or thing something comes from: the source of the problem.
Where something started; more formal.

ant.note: The cause comes first; the effect is what happens because of it.
What happens at the end because of the cause.

forms.definition: the process of one thing making another thing happen
forms.example: Scientists must prove causation, not only that two things happen together.

forms.definition: to make something happen, usually something bad
forms.example: Heavy rain caused floods in many villages.

syn.note: Easy and common: 'Smoking can lead to illness.'
Puts the focus on the result: 'The storm resulted in power cuts.'
Often used for big changes, good or bad.
To make something new; cause is usually about problems.

ant.note: To stop something bad from happening.

forms.definition: showing that one thing makes another thing happen
forms.example: Doctors found a causal link between smoking and heart disease.

forms.definition: in a way that shows one thing makes another happen
forms.example: The two problems are causally connected.
forms.note: Rare; used mostly in science and academic writing.

context.text: Doctors say that sugar causes many health problems. One common cause of tooth pain is sweet tea with lots of sugar.

reviewer_note: Verb corpus meaning; noun cause (reason) is a conversion. The 'good cause / charity' noun meaning is mentioned in a note only (same spelling).

corpus_definition: great care taken to avoid danger or mistakes

forms.definition: great care that you take to stay safe or avoid mistakes
forms.example: Drivers should use caution when the roads are icy.

syn.note: Easy, everyday word; caution is stronger and more formal.
Formal: careful and sensible thinking before you act.
Attention is about watching or listening closely, not always about danger.

ant.note: Not taking care, so mistakes or accidents happen.
Doing dangerous things without thinking about the risk.

forms.definition: to warn someone to be careful about a danger
forms.example: The guide cautioned us not to swim in the cold lake.

syn.note: Everyday word with the same meaning; caution is more formal.
To advise is to tell someone what you think they should do.

forms.definition: careful to avoid danger, risks or mistakes
forms.example: She is a cautious driver and never goes too fast.

syn.note: Easy word with almost the same meaning.
Careful because you don't trust a person or situation.
Formal: sensible and careful, especially with money.

ant.note: Not thinking enough about danger or mistakes.

forms.definition: giving a warning about a danger or a mistake
forms.example: Her story about losing all her savings is a cautionary tale.
forms.note: Most common in the phrase 'a cautionary tale'.

syn.note: Used before a noun with a similar meaning: a warning sign.

forms.definition: carefully, trying to avoid danger or mistakes
forms.example: The cat walked cautiously towards the big dog.

syn.note: Easy word with almost the same meaning.
Carefully, because you don't trust something.

ant.note: Without thinking about danger or mistakes.
In a dangerous way, without thinking.

context.text: The road to Chimgan was covered in snow, so my father drove cautiously. He is always cautious in winter and tells us to use caution near the mountains.

reviewer_note: cautious = caution + -ous (n dropped). incautious and cautiousness are rare and left out.

corpus_definition: A very famous person known to many people.

forms.definition: a very famous person, for example an actor, singer or sports star
forms.example: A celebrity from Tashkent opened the new shopping centre.

syn.note: Easy word, often used for actors, singers and sports players.
A famous person on TV or radio: a TV personality.
A very important person who gets special treatment; not always famous.
A very famous person who many people admire as a symbol of something.

ant.note: Informal: a person who is not famous or important: 'He was a nobody before the show.'

forms.definition: a very famous person, especially from TV, music or films
forms.example: The magazine is full of photos of celebs at parties.
forms.note: Short, informal form of the headword.
There is no verb made from this word.
There is no adjective made from this word.
There is no adverb in this family.

context.text: Many young people in Uzbekistan follow their favourite celebrity on Instagram. Some celebs share photos of their food and clothes every day.

reviewer_note: Person noun stays main noun entry. celebrate/celebrated share an old Latin root but are not made from celebrity, so they are not_family. Note: celebrated (= famous) is close in meaning.

corpus_definition: A formal event to celebrate something special.

forms.definition: a formal public event held for a special day or occasion
forms.example: They attended a graduation ceremony at the university yesterday.

syn.note: A celebration can be formal or informal; a ceremony is formal with fixed steps.
A set of actions always done in the same way, often religious.
General word for anything planned that happens.
A religious ceremony: a wedding service.

forms.note: There is no verb in this family.

forms.definition: used in or connected with a formal public event
forms.example: The guards wore ceremonial uniforms at the gate.

syn.note: Easy word; ceremonial is used for clothes or acts at a special event.
Done by people in authority, for example a government.

ant.note: Relaxed and everyday, not following special rules.

forms.definition: in a formal way that is part of a special event
forms.example: The new bridge was ceremonially opened by the mayor.
forms.note: Rare; mostly used in news reports.

syn.note: Easier word; in an official or formal way.

context.text: Our school held a big ceremony for the last day of classes. The teachers wore ceremonial gowns, and every student got a certificate.

reviewer_note: ceremonial = ceremony + -al (y to i). ceremonious (very polite and formal) is rare and left out.

corpus_definition: A difficult task that tests your ability to do something well.

forms.definition: a difficult task that tests how well you can do something
forms.example: Climbing the mountain was a real challenge for the whole team.

syn.note: Easy word; a challenge is usually harder and more exciting.
A difficulty is a problem; a challenge is a hard thing you try to do.
A piece of work; it can be easy or hard.
A hard experience that tests your strength or patience.

forms.definition: to test your skills or ability by being difficult
forms.example: This job challenges me every day, and I learn a lot.

syn.note: Easy word with a very close meaning.
To make someone use all their skill: 'This work really stretches me.'

forms.definition: to say or show that you think something is not right
forms.example: The student challenged the teacher's answer.
forms.note: Belongs to challenge = question or disagree, not a hard task.

forms.definition: difficult in a way that tests your ability and is interesting
forms.example: Learning Chinese is challenging but very exciting.

syn.note: Easy word; challenging sounds more positive.
Needs a lot of time, energy or skill.
Informal: hard to do.

forms.definition: having a disability or a special difficulty
forms.example: The school has special classes for physically challenged students.
forms.note: Belongs to challenge = a difficulty in life; a polite word used about disabilities.
There is no common adverb in this family.

people.definition: a person who tries to win a title from the winner
people.example: The young challenger beat the old champion in the final.
people.note: Belongs to challenge = invite someone to compete, not a hard task.

context.text: Moving to a new city was a big challenge for my sister. Her new job is challenging, but she says it challenges her to grow.

reviewer_note: Map keeps the 'hard task' meaning; challenge = question (verb) and challenger (competition) are other_meaning.

corpus_definition: The person who wins the first prize in a sport or activity.

forms.definition: a person or team that wins first place in a competition
forms.example: She is the national tennis champion this year.

syn.note: Easy word with the same meaning.
The person who holds the top title now; used in sport.
Literary or formal word for the person who wins.

ant.note: The person or team that does not win.
The person who comes second, just behind the winner.

forms.definition: a competition to find the best player or team
forms.example: Uzbekistan won the Asian football championship for young players.

syn.note: A series of games with many players or teams.
General word for any event where people try to win.
Often used for non-sport events: a singing contest.

forms.definition: to support and fight for an idea or a group of people
forms.example: She has championed women's rights for many years.
forms.note: Belongs to champion = a supporter of a cause, not a sports winner.
There is no adjective in this family.
There is no adverb in this family.

context.text: My cousin is a judo champion in Bukhara. Next month he will travel to Tashkent for the national championship.

reviewer_note: Person noun stays main noun entry; championship is the event noun. Verb champion (support a cause) is other_meaning.

corpus_definition: an organization that helps people who are in need.

forms.definition: a group that collects money or things to help people in need
forms.example: We gave our old toys to a local charity.

syn.note: An organization that gives money for good causes, often started by a rich person.
An organization that does not try to make money for its owners.
Help, like money or food, given to people who need it.
Very general word for any group of people working together.

forms.note: There is no verb in this family.

forms.definition: connected with helping poor people or people who need help
forms.example: She works for a charitable organization that helps sick children.

syn.note: Not run to make money; used for organizations.

ant.note: Run to make money, not to help people.

forms.definition: in a kind way, without judging other people badly
forms.example: Let's think charitably about his mistake; he was very tired.
forms.note: Belongs to charity = kindness towards others, not an organization.

context.text: Every Ramadan, our neighbours give food to a charity in the city. The charity sends it to families in need, and other charitable groups help too.

reviewer_note: Two corpus rows (same organization meaning) merged. charitably belongs to the 'kindness' meaning.
